chapter: Ch 4: Presentation and Disclosures Based Accounting Standards
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Applicability of AS 3 and Statutory Exemptions
topics.section: AS 3 / Section 129, Section 2(40) and Section 462 of Companies Act, 2013
explain: AS 3 is mandatory for Non-SMCs and Level I non-corporate entities, while encouraged for others.
Under the Companies Act 2013, all companies must prepare a Cash Flow Statement.
One Person Companies, Small Companies, and Dormant Companies are exempt under Section 129.
Private startup companies are also exempt via Section 462 notification.
Newly qualifying entities need not disclose previous year figures.
An enterprise previously qualifying but now disqualified must still prepare it for two more consecutive years.

flow.title: Applicability Determination Process
steps: Check if entity is Non-SMC or Level I
Apply mandatory AS 3 compliance
For companies, check Companies Act exemptions
Exempt OPC, Small, Dormant, and Startup Private
If disqualified, prepare for two more years

topics.example: A private tech startup registered under Section 462 does not need to attach a Cash Flow Statement with its annual financial filings.
remember: Exemption applies to OPC, Small Company, Dormant Company, and Start-up Private Company.
A disqualified entity continues preparing CFS for 2 consecutive years.
mistakes: Assuming all private companies are exempt from CFS; only eligible startup private companies qualify for this exemption.

quiz.q: Which of the following corporate entities is required to prepare a Cash Flow Statement under the Companies Act, 2013?
quiz.why: Public limited companies enjoy no statutory exemption from CFS preparation.

quiz.q: If an enterprise was qualified to prepare CFS last year but is now disqualified, it must continue preparing CFS for:
quiz.why: AS 3 mandates continued preparation for two consecutive years following disqualification.

topics.title: Meaning of Cash, Cash Equivalents, and Cash Flow
explain: Cash includes cash in hand and demand deposits with banks or financial institutions.
Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into known amounts of cash.
To qualify as a cash equivalent, an investment must have a maturity of 3 months or less from acquisition and insignificant risk of value change.
Investments in equity shares are normally excluded due to price volatility.
Cash flows are inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents.
Movements between cash and cash equivalents (like depositing cash into bank) are not cash flows.
Exchange differences on foreign currency balances are non-cash changes, not cash flows.

flow.title: Testing for Cash Equivalent
steps: Acquire short-term liquid investment
Check maturity from acquisition date
Is maturity 3 months or less?
Check for insignificant risk of value change
Classify as cash equivalent, not investing flow

topics.example: Depositing ₹10,000 physical currency into the company current account changes the components of cash, but results in zero cash flow.
remember: Maturity must be 3 months or less from date of acquisition.
Movements between cash components are not cash flows.
mistakes: Treating short-term equity share investments as cash equivalents; equity shares carry significant value risk and fail the test.

quiz.q: Which of the following is treated as a cash equivalent under AS 3?
o: Liquid equity shares of a listed company
Sovereign debt mutual fund units with 2-month maturity
Bank fixed deposit for a 2-year tenure
quiz.why: Debt instruments maturing within 3 months with insignificant value risk qualify as cash equivalents.

quiz.q: Depositing ₹50,000 cash in hand into a bank current account represents:
quiz.why: Movements between cash and cash equivalents do not generate any cash inflow or outflow.

topics.title: Classification of Cash Flows: Operating, Investing, and Financing
explain: Operating activities are the principal revenue-generating activities not falling under investing or financing.
Examples of operating flows: cash sales, collections from trade receivables, cash purchases, and operational overheads.
Investing activities involve acquiring and disposing of long-term assets and investments excluded from cash equivalents.
Examples of investing flows: buying/selling machinery, loans given to non-financial entities, and collecting investment income.
Financing activities alter the size and composition of owner equity and borrowings.
Examples of financing flows: issuing shares/debentures, bank loan repayments, and dividends paid.

flow.title: Activity Classification Test
steps: Identify the underlying transaction
Relates to equity capital or borrowings?
If yes, classify as Financing Activity
Relates to long-term assets or investments?
If yes, classify as Investing Activity
Otherwise, classify as Operating Activity

topics.example: Paying ₹4,00,000 to buy plant is an investing outflow, issuing ₹5,00,000 shares is a financing inflow, and collecting ₹3,50,000 from debtors is an operating inflow.
remember: Investing = Long-term assets & non-cash equivalent investments.
Financing = Equity, preference capital, and borrowings.
mistakes: Classifying dividends paid as an operating activity; dividends paid always represent a financing cash outflow.

quiz.q: Redemption of preference shares by an enterprise is classified as:
quiz.why: Redeeming preference share capital alters the enterprise's capital structure, making it a financing activity.

quiz.q: Cash received from trade receivables during the year is reported under:
quiz.why: Collections from trade receivables stem directly from the principal revenue-producing activities of the business.

topics.title: Specific Treatments: Financial Enterprises, Interest, Dividends, and Tax
explain: For financial enterprises, loans given/taken and interest/dividends received are operating activities.
For non-financial enterprises, interest paid is financing, while interest and dividends received are investing.
Dividends paid are strictly financing cash outflows for all enterprises.
TDS deducted on income is classified matching the nature of that underlying income.
Income tax paid on general operating income is an operating outflow unless specifically identified with investing/financing.
Advance tax paid specifically for capital gains on sale of fixed assets is an investing outflow.

flow.title: Interest and Dividend Classification
steps: Identify the item: Interest or Dividend
Is the enterprise a financial enterprise?
If yes, interest/dividend received is Operating
If non-financial, interest/dividend received is Investing
Interest paid by non-financial is Financing
Dividend paid is always Financing

topics.example: If a manufacturing company receives ₹68,000 interest after TDS of ₹8,200 on an investment, both gross receipt and TDS are presented under investing activities.
remember: Dividends paid = Financing for ALL enterprises.
Tax paid is Operating unless specifically identifiable with investing/financing.
mistakes: Classifying interest received by a commercial bank as an investing activity instead of an operating activity.

quiz.q: For a non-financial enterprise, interest received on debentures held as investments is classified as:
quiz.why: Holding debentures is an investment activity, so associated interest returns are investing inflows.

quiz.q: Where should advance tax paid on capital gains from the sale of fixed assets be classified?
quiz.why: Tax specifically linked to an investing asset transaction is classified under investing activities.

topics.title: Gross vs Net Basis and Non-Cash Transactions
explain: AS 3 prohibits netting off investing and financing receipts and payments unless exceptional criteria are met.
Netting is allowed for cash receipts/payments on behalf of customers (e.g., bank demand deposits).
Netting is also allowed for items where turnover is quick, amounts are large, and maturities are short.
Financial enterprises may report net flows for acceptance/repayment of fixed deposits, bank placements, and customer loans.
Transactions not involving cash or cash equivalents (e.g., issue of bonus shares, acquiring plant by issuing debentures) must be excluded from CFS.
Non-cash investing and financing activities must be disclosed elsewhere in the financial statements.

flow.title: Gross vs Net Reporting Decision
steps: Identify cash flow transaction
Does it involve actual cash exchange?
If no, exclude from CFS and disclose elsewhere
Is it on customer behalf or quick-turnover/short-maturity?
If yes, net reporting is permitted
Otherwise, report gross inflows and outflows separately

topics.example: Buying machinery for ₹25 lakhs and selling old furniture for ₹4 lakhs must be reported as gross outflow of ₹25 lakhs and gross inflow of ₹4 lakhs, never net ₹21 lakhs.
remember: Netting of fixed asset sales against purchases is strictly prohibited.
Bonus shares and shares/debentures issued for consideration other than cash are excluded from CFS.
mistakes: Netting machinery purchase against furniture sale to show a single net outflow figure.

quiz.q: Acquisition of plant by issuing 8% debentures worth ₹1,56,000 is reported in the Cash Flow Statement as:
o: Both investing outflow and financing inflow
Excluded from CFS and disclosed elsewhere
quiz.why: It is a non-cash transaction involving no flow of cash or cash equivalents; thus excluded from CFS.

quiz.q: Under AS 3, netting of cash receipts and payments is permitted for:
o: Issue and redemption of preference shares
Customer deposits accepted and repaid by banks
quiz.why: Transactions conducted on behalf of customers by financial enterprises can be reported on a net basis.

topics.title: Reporting Operating Flows: Direct vs Indirect Method
explain: Under the Direct Method, gross receipts from customers are offset against gross payments to suppliers, employees, and operating expenses.
Under the Indirect Method, net profit before tax is adjusted for non-cash items, non-operating items, and working capital changes.
Non-cash expenses like depreciation and provisions are added back under the indirect method.
Non-operating gains like profit on sale of fixed assets are deducted to isolate operating income.
Working capital adjustments exclude cash and cash equivalents.
Direct method is preferred by the standard because it shows clear sources and uses of operating cash.

flow.title: Indirect Method Reconciliation
steps: Start with Net Profit Before Tax
Add non-cash and non-operating expenses
Deduct non-operating incomes and gains
Adjust for changes in Working Capital
Deduct Income Tax paid
Arrive at Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities

topics.example: If net profit includes ₹50,000 depreciation and ₹8,000 gain on sale of equipment, add back ₹50,000 and deduct ₹8,000 when computing operating cash flows.
remember: Direct method shows gross operating cash flows.
Indirect method reconciles net profit to operating cash flow.
mistakes: Adjusting changes in cash and bank balances as part of working capital changes under the indirect method.

quiz.q: While computing operating cash flows under the indirect method, which of the following is deducted from net profit?
o: Gain on disposal of a fixed asset
Interest expense paid on bank loan
quiz.why: Gain on sale of fixed asset is an investing item and non-operating in nature; hence it must be deducted.

quiz.q: An entity sold equipment with a book value of ₹60,000 at a gain of ₹8,000. Under the direct method, the amount shown in operating activities is:
quiz.why: The entire ₹68,000 proceeds are an investing cash inflow; zero amount is reported under operating activities.

topics.title: Business Acquisitions, Disposals, and Foreign Currency Cash Flows
explain: Cash flows from acquiring or disposing of subsidiaries or business units must be classified under investing activities.
Receipts and payments for acquisitions and disposals cannot be netted against each other.
Current assets and liabilities taken over must be deducted from closing balances so working capital adjustments reflect operations only.
Foreign currency transactions are translated using the exchange rate at the transaction date.
Unrealised foreign exchange gains/losses on cash balances are non-cash items and excluded from cash flow totals.
The exchange difference is reported as a reconciling item in the notes reconciling opening and closing cash balances.

flow.title: Handling Foreign Currency Cash Balances
steps: Record opening foreign cash at opening rate
Translate foreign cash flows at transaction rates
Calculate closing foreign cash at closing rate
Compute unrealised exchange difference on opening/closing cash
Show exchange difference as reconciliation item in notes

topics.example: A bank holding €100,000 when the rate changes from ₹82 to ₹85 experiences an unrealised gain of ₹3,00,000, which is deducted from net profit and reconciled in notes.
remember: Business purchases/disposals belong strictly to Investing Activities.
Exchange differences on cash equivalents are non-cash reconciling items.
mistakes: Treating unrealised exchange gains on foreign currency bank accounts as operating or financing cash inflows.

quiz.q: Cash flows arising from the acquisition of a subsidiary company are presented under:
quiz.why: AS 3 specifically requires cash flows from business acquisitions to be classified as investing activities.

quiz.q: How is an unrealised exchange gain on a foreign currency bank balance presented in the CFS?
o: Reconciled in the notes to cash and cash equivalents
quiz.why: Unrealised exchange gains do not involve actual cash movements and are reported as a reconciling note item.
